businessModel: Regional facilities management services provider, 280 employees, $32M revenue

ownerIntake.businessType: Facilities management (HVAC, maintenance, cleaning) serving commercial real estate and corporate campuses across Southeast. $32M revenue, EBITDA 11.5% ($3.68M), down from 14% two years ago. Gross margin 28% (down from 31%). Labor cost increases (+14% in two years) outpacing pricing power.
ownerIntake.stage: Mature: margin compression and growth slowdown. Revenue +3% YoY (vs. 8% historical), EBITDA margin declining. Customer concentration: top 5 = 40% of revenue. Utilization 82% (tight), technician turnover 22% annually.
ownerIntake.ownerGoal: Restore EBITDA to 14%+ within 18 months through operational efficiency and customer mix optimization.
ownerConstraints: Labor shortage: technician wages +14% in 24 months; tight labor market. Automation capex needed but uncertain ROI.
Pricing pressure: Large customers (top 5 = 40% of revenue) push back on rate increases; price increases limited to 3-4% annually vs. cost increases 6%+ annually.
Service complexity: Customers expect higher service levels (faster response, higher quality) without paying premium. Scope creep consuming margin.
Competitive landscape: National FM companies entering markets with scale advantages; regional consolidation trend.
ownerIntake.immediateConcern: EBITDA margin eroding (14% → 11.5%) while revenue growth stalls (3% YoY vs. 8% historical). Labor cost inflation (+14%) outpaces pricing power (3-4%). Technician turnover (22%) increasing, creating training burden. Customer concentration (40%) creates risk. Must determine whether problem is pricing/customer mix or operational efficiency.

evidence.finding: EBITDA margin down 250bps (14% → 11.5%), gross margin down 300bps (31% → 28%). Revenue growth slowing (3% vs. 8% historical). Operating leverage negative: costs rising faster than revenue.
evidence.source: P&L trend analysis, two-year financial statements

evidence.finding: Labor costs +14% in 24 months while pricing power limited (3-4% annual increases). Technician turnover 22% consuming hiring/training resources.
evidence.source: Payroll data, pricing/contract analysis, HR turnover metrics

evidence.finding: Customer concentration is high: the top 5 customers represent 40% of the $32M revenue base, and these large accounts use their leverage to cap annual rate increases at 3-4% even as the firm's cost to serve rises 6%+ per year. Loss of any single top-5 account would remove roughly 8% of revenue, constraining the firm's willingness to push price and amplifying the margin squeeze.
evidence.source: Customer revenue analysis, contract renewal terms

evidence.finding: Technician utilization is tight at 82%, leaving little slack to absorb the 22% annual turnover, which forces continuous rehiring and training and pulls experienced technicians off billable work to onboard replacements. Compounding this, customers expect higher service levels (faster response, higher quality) without paying a premium, so scope creep consumes additional labor hours that are not recovered in price.
evidence.source: Workforce scheduling and utilization reports, service-level review

supportingData.scope_creep: Higher service expectations without premium pricing

evidence.finding: There is no per-customer or per-contract profitability reporting, so the firm cannot yet see which of its commercial real estate and corporate-campus accounts are contribution-positive versus negative after fully loaded technician labor, turnover-driven training cost, and scope-creep service hours. This blind spot means the 250bps EBITDA decline cannot be attributed to specific accounts or service lines without further analysis.
evidence.source: Finance team assessment; absence of contract-level cost accounting
